story.logline: A letter brings a test kit to your door. Most kits find nothing. Most people that the NHS asks to come in do not have cancer. What does the test change for you?

question: Should I do the NHS bowel screening home test each time it arrives?

source.title: Bowel cancer screening
quotes: Bowel cancer screening is currently offered to people aged 50 to 74 every 2 years.
You collect the sample at home and send it by post to be tested.
If your result says you need further tests it means blood was found in your poo and needs to be investigated.
You'll usually need to have a colonoscopy, which is where a camera is used to check inside your bowel.
If blood is found in your poo, it does not always mean you have cancer.
Even if bowel cancer screening shows you do not need further tests, it does not always mean you do not have bowel cancer.

Northern Ireland: people aged 60 to 74 years who are registered with a GP.
Your test kit (FIT kit) should include a sample bottle, an envelope, and instructions on how to do the test.
Write the date on the sample bottle.
Open the sample bottle and remove the lid, which has a sample stick attached.
Gently scrape the end of the sample stick along your poo until all the grooves are covered. Only a small amount is needed.
Put the sample stick back into the sample bottle and close the lid tightly.
Put the sample bottle in the envelope included in your test kit and seal it.
Post the envelope with your sample as soon as you can. Postage is free and you do not need a stamp.
You'll usually get the results of your bowel cancer screening home test (FIT kit) within 2 weeks after sending your poo sample. Sometimes it can take longer.
You'll be invited to an appointment with a specialist nurse who will talk with you about your results, and what happens next.

simulate.prompt: Try your age, your choice about a colonoscopy, and how often kits find blood.

tradeoffs: More kits give you more chances to find cancer or polyps early. They also bring more letters that ask you to come in for more tests. Most of those tests find no cancer.

A colonoscopy looks for the cause of the blood. It can often remove polyps at the same time. But first you take laxatives to empty your bowel. Then you go to hospital. There is a small risk: about 1 in 1,700 colonoscopies tears the bowel.
You do the kit at home and post it free. But it can miss a polyp or cancer that did not bleed that day. So an all-clear letter is not a guarantee.
leftOut: The crowd counts what the tests find, not the lives they save. A review of trials of an older kit found it avoided about 1 in 6 bowel cancer deaths. This page has no figure like that for today's kit.

The model gives every kit the same chance to find blood, whatever earlier kits showed. In real life, people with cancer or high-risk polyps stop the home kits. They get hospital care or check-up colonoscopies instead.

The NHS gives two figures for kits that find blood. The leaflet says around 2 to 3 in 100. The programme's 2024-25 data say 1.71 in 100. The model uses the newer figure. Move the slider to see the older one.
The colonoscopy results use the NHS leaflet's rough shares for everyone. Your own chances depend on your age, sex, family history and health.
It leaves out symptoms. Anyone with symptoms of bowel cancer should see a GP, whatever their last kit said.
It covers England's programme. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland run their own programmes. Northern Ireland starts at 60.
